topic: NYCB losses, commercial real estate, and regional-bank contagion
capture_method: curator-frozen extracts plus contemporaneous market observations

extracts: NYCB recorded a $552 million provision for credit losses versus $62 million in Q3 and $185 million of net charge-offs, driven by two loans.
Non-performing assets were 0.38% of assets; the allowance was $992 million and 232% of non-performing loans.
The common dividend was cut to $0.05 as the bank accelerated capital building after crossing $100 billion in assets.
Market contacts viewed CRE as a potential stress trigger because of rates, lower property values, and structural office-demand changes.
Small and regional banks were viewed as more vulnerable because of higher CRE concentration, but vulnerability is not the same as insolvency for every institution.
Noncurrent non-owner-occupied CRE loans rose 36.4% sequentially and the noncurrent rate was the highest since Q3 2014.
Industry unrealized securities losses were $683.9 billion, while deposit outflows were moderating.
The report described emerging office stress and funding pressure, not a conclusion of system-wide failure.

sources.publisher: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
extracts: The OCC said credit risk was increasing due partly to higher rates and CRE, while the overall federal banking system remained sound.
The combination argues for institution-level funding, capital, concentration, and loan-quality analysis rather than a blanket sector verdict.

sources.publisher: Yahoo Finance and contemporaneous exchange archives
sources.notes: NYCB later completed a reverse split; 4.90 is the contemporaneous pre-split price convention.
